text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--The new Amsterdam treaty has adopted the Danish EU optouts and strengthened environmental regulations the (far-left) Socialist Peoples' Party should therefore vote for its acceptance at a referendum next year, say party vice-chair Christine Antorini and EU spokesman Joern Jespersen. Both say, however that the party has not yet made a final decision.
--A new survey shows that two out of three Danes believe that institutional investors should take a company's ethics into account when considering investing in it.

--Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen has launched a counter-offensive against Greenland Prime Minister Lars Emil Johansen saying that he has completely ignored formal Danish-Greenland joint working bodies with his surprise offer to store decomissioned U.S. and Russian nuclear weapons in Greenland (a self-governing territory of Denmark, which retains control over defence and foreign affairs).

--With U.S. President Bill Clinton expected to visit Denmark on July 10/11 the Danish government has still not received firm confirmation of the dates and has heard nothing from the White House since a planned earlier visit was cancelled in March due to Clinton's knee injury.

--Government plans to raise a labour market levy to 12 percent from eight percent is an attack on Danes' savings for their old age, and will send one crown in seven now going into capital pension plans to state coffers instead, says insurance company Danica
--A boom in the Danish data-processing industry means that temporary staff are being imported from Norway and employment agencies are setting up specialist data departments.
--Danish Exports to Britain are falling, despite the strong pound which makes Danish goods cheaper, but still unable to compete on price with competitors like Sweden and the Netherlands.
